state.title: docs(session): clarify primed_at as delivery-attempted, not consumed (#5236)
state.body:
Fixes #5236.

## What's misleading

`primed_at` is stamped when delivery was *selected and runtime start succeeded* — but several doc comments described this as "confirmed delivered" / "actually delivers," which reads as proof the agent consumed the prompt. It isn't proof of that: the issue's own qualifying incident had a worker holding `primed_at` while its trigger bead stayed open/unassigned until a manual nudge forced the claim.

## Fix — comment/doc-string only, zero behavior or schema change

- `internal/session/lifecycle_transition.go` — `PrimedAtMetadataKey`'s doc said "confirmed delivered" with no caveat; added that "confirmed" means transport succeeded, not consumption, and pointed at trigger-bead assignment as the real work-started signal.
- `cmd/gc/prompt_delivery.go` — `promptDeliveryResult`/`Delivered` docs said "actually delivered it," but `promptDelivery()` does no I/O at all (pure routing decision, per its own existing doc) — clarified `Delivered` means "a mechanism was selected."
- `cmd/gc/session_lifecycle_parallel.go` — `promptDelivered` field doc said "actually delivers the rendered startup prompt" (one of the issue's own evidence citations) — same fix.

**Deliberately left `session_level_converge.go` untouched**, even though it also uses "CONFIRMED" language for `primedAt`: that's the S19 Stage-1 migration module ("nothing reads the action list yet ... until Stage 3 wires the act loop"), and its terminology is already precisely scoped within its own durable-world/runtime-world framework — it separately tracks `primedEnv` as "delivered this runtime but may not yet be durably recorded," meaning it already distinguishes the two states this issue wants clarified. Touching an in-progress migration module's carefully-established vocabulary without Stage 3/4 context felt like the wrong call. `internal/runtime/herdr/provider.go` (the issue's other evidence citation) was already correctly worded — no change needed there either.

## Verification

`go test ./internal/session/... -run 'Primed|Priming|Prompt'` and `go test ./cmd/gc/... -run 'PromptDelivery|Primed|Priming'` both green (comment-only, no regressions); gofmt clean; `go vet` clean on changed + dependent packages; `go build ./...` clean.

state.title: docs: define the Gas City identity separator contract

## What this changes

Gas City now has an authoritative reference for how qualified Agent identities become tmux-safe session names: `/` encodes as `--`, while `.` encodes as `__`. The new page is linked from the specifications index and documentation navigation, and the source implementation points maintainers back to the written contract.

The contract also documents the current Beads comparison behavior and its version boundary. This is a documentation and contract-test change only; it does not alter runtime identity handling or update the Beads dependency.

## Review notes

- Review `docs/reference/specs/identity-separator-contract-v1.md` for the two-axis encoding, worked examples, and the distinction between Gas City minting identities and Beads comparing them.
- The Beads section deliberately calls out that Gas City's pinned Beads version predates the cited upstream canonicalizer; that caveat should remain until the dependency advances and the behavior is re-verified.
- `internal/agent/session_name.go` changes only its explanatory comment. The two new tests protect the document's presence, source link, and required contract terms.

## Test plan

- [x] Run `go build ./...` and `go vet ./...`.

state.title: feat(controller): poke the reconciler on provider session events instead of waiting for the next patrol scan
state.body:
## What this changes

A session that dies is noticed when the controller's patrol next scans for it. A provider
that pushes session events already knows seconds earlier, and nothing consumed that. This
adds one consumer: `cmd/gc/session_event_pump.go` bridges the provider's event stream into
the session reconciler's existing poke channel.

herdr implements `runtime.SessionEventProvider`, so it gets this. tmux has no stream and
is untouched. Patrol cadence is unchanged, the reconciler's behavior is unchanged, and
there is no new configuration. The reconcile simply runs sooner, on a signal that was
already arriving and being dropped.

## How it behaves

The pump is level-triggered throughout: an event is a hint to go look, never a fact to act
on.

- Attributed `exited` and `closed` events poke immediately.
- Resync events poke on a trailing delay (15s, re-armed per resync). Every connection
  cycle leads with a resync, including the benign resubscribe the stream runs for each
  newly detected agent pane, and an immediate poke would land a reconcile inside the very
  start wave that triggered it.
- One minute after the first resync of a burst, the poke lands regardless. The last re-arm
  is clamped to what remains of that window, so the cap is the poke's deadline rather than
  the point after which one more whole delay may still run.
- Unattributed pane events are dropped. Such a poke races an in-flight create's metadata
  stamp and rolls the pending create back.

The pump deliberately publishes no "the stream is healthy" signal. herdr's
`SubscribeSessionEvents` returns a channel and a nil error unconditionally and connects
behind it, retrying forever with capped backoff, so a subscription to an unreachable
provider is indistinguishable from a live one. `streaming()` documents that, and says
outright that it must not be used to decide to poll less: a stream that exists is not a
stream that has delivered.

## What is deliberately not here

**Delivering queued nudges on idle events.** That consumer was written, reviewed, and then
removed from this change. Routing every delivery through one shared worker turns a
per-session hang into a city-wide one: `runtime.Provider.Nudge` takes no context at all,
herdr's implementation uses `context.Background()`, and the client applies no timeout, so a
hung prompt would block delivery for every other session and ignore cancellation. The
per-session pollers that exist today confine that blast radius. Retiring them is only safe
once each delivery is bounded and the worker can abandon a hung one, which is a change of
its own.

**A `[daemon].session_patrol_interval` that stretched the patrol while events were
flowing.** Also written, also removed. The run loop cancels pending event-driven fires on
every patrol tick, and says why in a comment: a patrol scans every reconciler state
authoritatively. A patrol that skips the session phases makes that false, so a death poke
armed a second before a patrol was cancelled by a patrol that then did not scan, and
detection waited for the stretched interval. It was an optimisation layered on a feature
that is worth having without it.

## One unrelated test

`TestNewCityRuntimeWiresAssignedWorkDeferTracker`. The assigned-work defer tracker is
constructed in `newCityRuntime` and consumed through an option, and every test for it
drives the option directly, so dropping the construction leaves the suite green while the
backstop is dead in production. That happened during this work, and only the unused-symbol
linter caught it, because the builder lost its last caller at the same moment; losing just
the call would have been silent.

The test asserts both halves, and it pins the production call site through `go/parser`
rather than a text search. A text search cannot tell code from a comment, so commenting
the argument out would leave the backstop dead with the test still green.

## Test plan

- `gofmt`, `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`: clean.
- `go test ./internal/config/ ./internal/session/ ./internal/runtime/herdr/... ./internal/testpolicy/... ./test/docsync/`: pass.
- `go test ./cmd/gc/`: pass (279s).
- `make check-docs`: pass.
- `golangci-lint run ./cmd/gc/... ./internal/config/... ./internal/session/... ./internal/runtime/herdr/...`: clean.
- Live journey against herdr 0.8.0 (`make test-herdr-live`, which now covers the `cmd/gc`
  journey as well): an agent's natural process exit lands a reconcile poke with no polling.
  The opt-in predicate and the single subprocess the live tier shells out to moved into
  `internal/runtime/herdr/herdrtest` so the provider tier and `cmd/gc` share one gate and
  one bounded polling helper. Each `report-agent` invocation is bounded at 2s, because an
  unbounded call inside the helper's poll condition would mean its 10s bound was never
  reachable and a hung server would surface as the outer test timeout instead.
- No test sleeps. The pump's timer behavior runs inside `testing/synctest` bubbles, where
  the trailing-delay and cap assertions are exact rather than approximate.
- Mutation checks on the wiring guard: deleting the tracker argument fails the test,
  commenting it out fails it, and the real code passes.

state.title: fix(mail): supersede recurring digests and retire resolved BLOCKED reports
state.body:
## Problem

The mayor inbox accumulates and never drains, so it stops carrying signal. On
2026-09-15 it grew from 27 to 32 unread messages in one afternoon: 15 BLOCKED
worker reports, 6 hourly Slack alert review digests, and 11 one-off
completions. Two distinct causes, fixed as two separable commits.

1. A recurring order reports **full current state** every hour, so six copies
   of the same state are noise and only the newest matters.
2. A BLOCKED report whose blocker is already cleared stays unread forever.
   `sc-wisp-chkxapn` asked for PR 25 to be merged, which happened;
   `sc-wisp-3d8v85a` asked for the launchd agent to be enabled, which
   happened. Both reports are still sitting there.

## What changes

### `gc mail send --supersede <order>`

A recurring digest names its order. The new message archives the sender's
earlier **unread** messages carrying the same key to the **same** recipient.
Archiving closes the message bead and retains its body, so a superseded digest
stays readable through `gc mail peek` and `bd show` — no history is deleted.

The match is scoped by key, sender, and recipient together, and skips messages
already read. A worker's one-off report carries no key, so no later digest can
retire it.

### `gc mail send --blocked-on <bead>`

An escalation names the bead it waits on. The reader's next `gc mail inbox`
archives the report once that bead closes.

**Mechanism chosen: an explicit annotation plus a sweep on the inbox read
path.** Alternatives rejected:

- **Scrape bead ids out of the subject and body.** Rejected. A message that
  mentions a closed bead in passing would be archived, and the failure mode is
  exactly the one that must never happen: a live escalation disappears. The bead
  description notes that five notices today already named session beads rather
  than messages, which is what text scraping produces.
- **Hook `gc bd close` to archive the mail.** Rejected. It couples the close
  path to the mail package for no gain, and it misses every close that goes
  through `bd` directly rather than `gc bd` — which on this machine is most of
  them.
- **Auto-archive on a timer.** Explicitly forbidden by the bead, and rightly:
  age is not evidence that a blocker is resolved.

The sweep acts only on positive evidence. A bead still open or in progress, a
bead the store cannot read, and a named session or message bead all keep the
report visible. A session bead closes when its session ends, which says nothing
about the blocker. The sweep is advisory: a failure warns on stderr and never
stops the listing, because a stale report beats no listing at all.

A backend that cannot carry metadata rejects both flags rather than dropping
them. A digest whose supersede key vanished would pile up again with no sign
that anything failed.

### Incidental

`cmdMailSend` is gone. It existed only to pass `jsonOut=false` from a branch in
`RunE`, which now passes the flag straight through, leaving the wrapper with no
production caller (`unparam` flagged it).

## Tests

Each acceptance criterion has a test that fails when its guard is removed.

| Test | Proves |
|---|---|
| `TestSupersedeKeyLeavesOnlyTheNewestDigestUnread` | A second digest from the same order to the same recipient leaves exactly **one** unread message, the retained unread body is the **newest**, and the older one is closed with its body intact. |
| `TestSupersedeNeverRetiresUnrelatedMessages` | A one-off worker report, a different order, a different sender, and a different recipient all survive. Six sends, four survivors. |
| `TestArchiveResolvedBlockersOnlyRetiresClosedBlockers` | A message naming a still-open bead, an unknown bead, a closed **session** bead, or no bead at all is never archived. Only the closed work bead's report goes. |
| `TestArchiveResolvedBlockersSkipsReadAndRepeats` | A read message is left alone, and a repeat sweep is a no-op. |
| `TestSendAnnotatedMail*` (3) | The flags reach the message as the keys the backend reads back; a backend without metadata support rejects rather than drops; unannotated mail keeps the plain `Send` path. |
| `TestSweepResolvedBlockersPassesEveryRecipientRoute` | Every resolved recipient route is swept; a provider without the extension is skipped silently; a sweep failure warns but does not fail the listing. |

Mutation check on the guard the criteria hinge on: replacing the key-and-sender
comparison in `supersedePrior` with `if false` makes
`TestSupersedeNeverRetiresUnrelatedMessages` fail with
`unread subjects = [review: second], want 4 messages`.

```
go test ./internal/mail/... ./cmd/gc/ -run 'Mail|Nudge|Supersede|ResolvedBlockers|SendAnnotatedMail|SessionModelPhase0' -count=1   # ok
go test ./internal/api/... ./internal/bootstrap/... -count=1                                                                        # ok
golangci-lint run internal/mail/... cmd/gc/...   # clean, except a pre-existing revive hit in dolt_data_dir_lock_other.go
```

## Overlap with open PRs

Checked 6358, 6371, and 6372 as the bead asked.

- **6358** (`Reject non-message mail mutations`) touches `beadmail.go`, but only
  adds type guards inside `Read`, `MarkRead`, and `MarkUnread`. This PR touches
  `Send` and adds new functions. No conflict, and the two are complementary.
- **6371** is supervisor/launchd only.
- **6372** touches `cmd_nudge.go` and the pending-mail notice, not the send or
  inbox paths changed here.

## Follow-up, not in this PR

`scripts/slack-alert-review.py` in the Stryker-City workspace needs
`--supersede slack-alert-review` added to its `gc mail send` call for the fix to
take effect on the six digests that motivated it. That file sits outside this
repository and another session holds a live claim on it.

Closes sc-rur0b.

state.title: cmd-gc-productmetrics-testhook runs at 92-95% of its 5-minute budget on main; its six tests take 0.87s and the rest is compile
state.body:
## Symptom

`cmd-gc-productmetrics-testhook` runs at 92–95% of its `timeout-minutes: 5` budget on `main`, so it fails as a cancellation ("The operation was canceled") on whichever PR happens to add a few seconds. It is a required-path job, so that reads as a red gate with no failing test in the log.

Measured across runs on 2026-09-16 (UTC):

| branch | duration |
|---|---|
| `main` @ `9700d9a48` | 4m37 |
| a branch with no `go.mod` change | 4m44 |
| a branch that changed `go.sum` | **5m05 → killed** |

## Root cause

The budget is buying compile time, not test time, on a runner the budget was not sized for.

From the job's own timing artifact (`timing-cmd-gc-productmetrics-testhook-attempt-1`, run 35040648087, `main` @ `9700d9a48`):

- `cmd/gc` package unit: **0.869 s**
- every test in it: sub-second; six tests, **0.87 s total**

against a 4m37 job. The remainder is `go build` of `cmd/gc` under `-tags productmetrics_testhook`.

The job requests `runs-on: ${{ needs.runner-policy.outputs.runner_32vcpu }}` (`.github/workflows/ci.yml:626`), but `runner-policy` resolves that to `ubuntu-latest` for every login outside the maintainer list — the same artifact's runner block reports `"cpu_count": 4`. So most runs compile `cmd/gc` on four cores inside a five-minute wall.

The `go.sum` sensitivity follows: `actions/setup-go`'s cache key includes `go.sum`, so any dependency change makes that build cold, and cold is what goes over.

## Reproduction

Open a PR that changes `go.sum` at all, on a fork or from a non-maintainer login, and watch `cmd/gc product metrics testhook`. Or read the timing artifact of any recent `main` run and compare the summed test durations against the job duration.

## Environment

`main` @ `9700d9a48`, `ubuntu-latest` (4 vCPU), `actions/setup-go@4a36011`, Go per `go.mod`.

## Proposed fixes, either

1. **Give the job a warm build cache.** It is the only `cmd/gc`-building job with no warm step before it; the surrounding jobs go through `setup-gascity-ubuntu`. That attacks the 4m23 rather than the wall.
2. **Size the budget for the runner the job actually gets** — 10–12 minutes gives real margin at 4 vCPU.

(1) is the better fix; (2) is the one-line stopgap. A gate at 95% of budget reports on runner speed rather than on the code.

state.title: perf(gc): probe bd context once per TTL instead of once per store open (cr-uavzft)
state.body:
Every gc CLI call opens several stores, and each open ran the beads storage
preflight, which unconditionally forked 'bd <scope> context --json' to ask what
backend the process was about to open (cr-m3g3od measured 4 children for one
'gc bd show'). The answer - backend, dolt_mode, bd_version, schema_version - is
process-static inside any window the call lives in, so read it once per
(city, scope) and reuse it.

Only a success is recorded and the entry is aged by a TTL, so a bd that is
unreachable, uninstalled, or mid-upgrade still fails the preflight closed on
every later check, and a long-lived controller re-probes instead of carrying a
boot-time answer forever. The per-entry mutex is held across the probe, so
concurrent opens of one scope collapse into a single spawn.

Same shape gc already uses for the city-scoped storage routes
(cli_storage_routes.go), and consistent with its position on this probe in a
poll path (api_state_conditional_writes.go: 'a status poll must not shell out
to bd').

Bead: cr-uavzft
(cherry picked from commit 4d18e29d55adb25a4e6a4ee03e4d5a1b6841d198)

Staged and tested in the westlands estate (bead cr-uavzft); tests green on the estate builders.

state.title: bug: pool seats retired mid-claim because alias-form claims are invisible to the keep-awake and drain-ack close gates
state.body:
### Gas City version
main `ed146d8d9` (2026-09-02); the unit-level reproduction also holds on `af596339d` (2026-09-14).

### Environment
Linux (Fedora 44), tmux runtime, opencode-backed pool agents (gastown pack `gastown.polecat`, `max_active_sessions = 10`).

### Reproduction
1. Route several beads to a pool template; seats claim them with `gc hook --claim`. The claim's `assignee` is the seat alias (`GC_ALIAS`, e.g. `rig/gastown.nux`), while the session bead's `session_name` is the tmux form (`rig--gastown__nux`).
2. Let template demand drop (other beads finish) while one seat still holds an `in_progress` claim.
3. Watch the reconciler: that seat is closed with `session drained: pool slot retired by reconciler`, followed immediately by `bead.dead_assignee_reopened` for its claim, and a fresh seat re-primes from zero.

### Expected behavior
A seat holding an `in_progress` claim stays desired (`assigned-work`), is counted by `countAssignedScaleSlots`, and the drain-ack close gate sees its claim.

### Actual behavior
`sessionAssignmentIdentifierRaw`/`RawInfo` and `ComputeAwakeSet`'s `sessionAssigneeMatches` only compare `{bead id, session_name, configured named identity}`. Claims are written under the alias (`session.AssigneeIdentifier` is alias-first), so every pool seat reads as work-free and becomes a scale-down victim. The orphan-release path (`session.AssigneeIdentities`) already honours the alias, which is why the reopen follows the drain within seconds.

### Logs, screenshots, or traces
One city, 24 h, tributary pool: 122 polecat stops, 89 `bead.dead_assignee_reopened`, mean seat life ~20 min, 15–25 % of seats under 3 min; identical under three model providers, so not model-related. With the alias honoured in those three sites (see the linked PR): 22 stops and 0 reopens over the next 24 h.

### Additional context
`TestAssignmentGuardsIgnoreTransientPoolSlotAliases` states slot-form aliases (`<pool>-<n>`) must never keep a session alive. The PR keeps that guard and honours namepool aliases only. If the preferred fix is to claim under a stable identity instead (bead id / session_name), I'm happy to rework it that way.

state.title: bug: a requested named-session restart can leave a live, promptless runtime — start errors in start_call, never reaches post_start_observe, and nothing retries
state.body:
### Before you continue

- [x] I searched existing issues and did not find a duplicate.
- [x] I read the relevant docs and contributor guidance.

Searched: `resuming session: session already exists`, `post_start_observe`,
`restart-requested no such session`, `session reconciler race prompt`,
`session launched without prompt`, `unprimed session`,
`start_call provider_error session already exists`.

The two nearest hits are **not** this, and I want to be explicit about why,
because both look close:

- **#5593** (closed) matches on the error string `resuming session: session
  already exists`, but it is about `one_shot` **pool** sessions blocking their
  own runtime name after a normal exit. This is a **named** session being
  restarted on request.
- **#4382** (open) is also "born unprimed", but by a different mechanism:
  reconciler-spawned **formula step** sessions whose routing is stamped at
  `bead.created` so `nudge-on-route` never fires. Here the session is a named
  one, the restart was explicitly requested, and the start itself errors.

### Gas City version

`HEAD-e736d74d0` — source build of `e736d74d0` (2026-08-24), with a
source-built `bd` `1.1.0 (dev: main@bf97b73749ac)`.

### Environment

Linux, systemd `--user` supervisor, Dolt-backed stores, `claude` provider,
2 rigs (both suspended — a near-idle city). Named session `mayor`,
`lifecycle` restart-on-request via `gc handoff`.

### Reproduction

1. Have a named, controller-restartable session (here: `mayor`).
2. From inside it, request a restart — `gc handoff`, which sends mail to self
   and then `gc runtime request-restart`.
3. Observe the reconciler's stop/start pair in `supervisor.log`.

It does not reproduce on demand: this is a **race**, and it has now happened
twice in twelve days against ~119 healthy starts in the same log. I am filing
it because both occurrences leave the *same* distinctive signature, so the
signature is probably more useful to you than a recipe.

### Expected behavior

The restarted session receives its rendered template prompt as the first user
message, as it does on every healthy start.

### Actual behavior

The runtime starts and the prompt is never delivered. A `claude` process is
alive in the tmux session, attached and idle, with **zero user records in its
transcript**, and it stays that way indefinitely — 7m08s on this occurrence,
until a human ran `gc session reset mayor`. 15 minutes on the previous one.

Nothing retries: the session is up, so the reconciler is satisfied.

### Logs, screenshots, or traces

The failing restart, `~/.gc/supervisor.log`:

```
session reconciler: clearing restart-requested marker for mayor (bead bl-0odu):
    tmux -u: no such session: mayor
Stopped restart-requested session 'mayor'
session reconciler: provider-health registry unavailable for "claude-mayor";
    treating as green
session lifecycle: op=start wave=0 session=mayor template=mayor
    outcome=start_enqueued duration=0s
session reconciler: starting mayor: resuming session: session already exists:
    session "mayor"
session lifecycle: op=start wave=0 session=mayor template=mayor
    outcome=provider_error duration=351ms phases=[start_call=351ms]
    err=resuming session: session already exists: session "mayor"
Stopped restart-requested session 'mayor'
```

The successful manual reset seven minutes later, same session, same log:

```
session lifecycle: op=start wave=0 session=mayor template=mayor
    outcome=start_enqueued duration=0s
Woke session 'mayor'
session lifecycle: op=start wave=0 session=mayor template=mayor
    outcome=success duration=19.799s
    phases=[start_call=17.727s post_start_observe=2.072s]
```

**The discriminator is `post_start_observe`.** Every healthy start in this log
carries it (~5s + ~2.1s); the failed start has only `start_call` and no `Woke
session` line. The prompt appears to be delivered in that phase, so a start
that errors in `start_call` leaves a live, promptless runtime behind.

The 2026-09-04 occurrence has the same shape with a different error string —
`outcome=success duration=28ms phases=[start_call=28ms]`, no
`post_start_observe` — against ~5s + ~2.1s on the other 118 starts in that
window.

The event log tells the same story more compactly. A requested restart emits
`session.draining` then `session.woke`; across nine prior restarts of this
session the pair is always 32–68s apart, and on the failure the second event
never arrives:

```
14:55:08 -> 14:55:40  +32s      21:00:26 -> 21:01:02  +36s
15:14:44 -> 15:15:52  +68s      21:37:15 -> 21:37:49  +34s
16:39:43 -> 16:40:38  +55s      00:13:45 -> 00:14:44  +59s
18:38:57 -> 18:39:54  +57s      10:09:49 -> (none)
19:11:15 -> 19:11:52  +37s
```

### Additional context

**The apparent mechanism**, offered as a reading of the log rather than as a
claim about the code, which I have not read: the reconciler goes to clear the
restart marker and tmux reports the session already gone. Its bookkeeping then
treats the session as present on the following start — the start takes a
*resume* path — and the resume errors because by then a tmux session named
`mayor` exists again.

**Two things that might matter for the fix:**

1. `provider_error` here is not retried. Whatever the right recovery is, the
   current outcome is a permanently idle session that looks healthy to
   everything watching it.
2. `gc session reset` is a reliable recovery, and we have automated it locally
   behind a zero-user-records predicate. That is a workaround, not a fix, and
   it only works because a session with no user records has no state to lose.

**A detail that may help anyone else hitting this:** a queued nudge cannot
rescue such a session. Ours were dead-lettered with `queued nudge session
fence mismatch` about 29s in — the fence is the continuation epoch rather than
the session id, so a nudge queued across the restart boundary dies with the
old epoch. So the failure is not observable-and-recoverable through the nudge
path; the session has to be replaced.
